id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05634v8
published: 2025-07-08T03:29:16Z
summary: Consider sequential binary testing under model uncertainty or misspecification in an otherwise 'ideal' setting: the a posteriori belief process and its objective conditional probability counterpart may differ but converge to the same correct outcome. We show that under common conditions (defined) unless the two are 'essentially identical', differing only by a priori factors, time-homogeneous continuous decisions based on one must fail to be path-independent with respect to state-variables based on the other or any non-essentially-identical process. The difference between them, inferential error, decomposes uniquely into two independent components: a path-independent systematic bias and a path-dependent, not necessarily systematic, error.

title: The Wellposedness of Path-dependent Multidimensional Forward-backward SDE
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/1908.09208v3
published: 2019-08-24T21:02:09Z
summary: We study in this paper the wellposedness of path-dependent multidimensional forward-backward stochastic differential equations (FBSDE). By path-dependent we mean that the coefficients of the forward-backward SDE at time t can depend on the whole path of the forward process up to time t. These kinds of forward-backward SDE appear when solving path-dependent stochastic control problem by means of variational calculus. At the heart of our analysis is the construction of a decoupling random field on the path space. We first prove the existence and the uniqueness of decoupling field on small time interval. Then by introducing the characteristic BSDE, we show that a global decoupling field can be constructed by patching local solutions together as long as the solution of the characteristic BSDE remains bounded. Finally, we show that the solution of a path-dependent forward-backward SDE is stable.

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=theoretical+frameworks+for+artificial+moral+agency+and+responsibility+attribution+in+autonomous+systems&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7473639\", \"title\": [\"Artificial Intelligence and Legal Responsibility: Agency, Causal Attribution, Foreseeability and the Reconstruction of Liability in Autonomous Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Contemporary liability doctrine addresses artificial intelligence through three analytically separate inquiries: agency doctrine, which asks who authorized an act; causal-attribution doctrine, which asks what produced a harm; and foreseeability doctrine, which asks what a reasonable actor should have anticipated. Each inquiry anchors its analysis to a different moment in a system's lifecycle-delegation, harm, and design, respectively. For conventional tools this temporal separation is harmless because a single human actor typically occupies all three positions at once. Autonomous systems break that coincidence: the interval between design, delegation, and harm now contains machine-generated intervening choices that no human actor directly authorized, observed, or could fully anticipate. This article develops the thesis that recent liability reforms-the European Union's Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853, the United Kingdom's Automated Vehicles Act 2024, the Republic of Korea's Basic Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of a Foundation for Trust, and Brazil's pending Marco Legal da Inteligência Artificial (PL 2338/2023)-each stabilize only one of these three temporal anchors without reconciling how the anchors interact when a single harm implicates all three simultaneously. Using doctrinal and comparative legal analysis across these four jurisdictions plus United States tort doctrine, the article identifies this structural problem as temporal anchor divergence: the three liability inquiries increasingly point to different responsible parties for the same harm rather than converging on one, and current reforms treat this divergence as an implementation detail rather than a problem requiring an explicit resolution rule.
